intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PRPH2 gene (179605) on chromosome 6p21.1. Digenic RP7 is caused by double heterozygous mutation in the PRPH2 and ROM1 genes. Homozygous mutation in PRPH2 has also been found in patients with juvenile RP.

checks.claim: Retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PRPH2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We report here three mutations of the human homologue of the rds gene (RDS) that cosegregate with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa in separate families.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports RDS mutations causing autosomal dominant RP. It does not explicitly state that the mutations are heterozygous; dominant inheritance only implies it.

checks.claim: The PRPH2 gene is located on chromosome 6p21.1.
checks.evidence_quote: We report here three mutations of the human homologue of the rds gene (RDS)
checks.explanation: The abstract does not give the chromosome location. It is accepted here under the rule that a gene's standard chromosomal location restates the paper.

checks.claim: Digenic RP7 is caused by double heterozygous mutation in the PRPH2 and ROM1 genes.
checks.evidence_quote: Three families were identified with mutations in the unlinked photoreceptor-specific genes ROM1 and peripherin/RDS, in which only double heterozygotes develop retinitis pigmentosa (RP).
checks.explanation: The abstract says digenic RP occurs in people who are double heterozygous for ROM1 and peripherin/RDS (PRPH2) mutations. 'RP7' is OMIM's label for this disease.

checks.claim: Homozygous mutation in PRPH2 has been found in patients with juvenile retinitis pigmentosa.
checks.evidence_quote: found the same homozygous missense mutation p.L185P in PRPH2 in a third juvenile RP patient, 741
checks.explanation: Juvenile RP patient 741 was homozygous for a PRPH2 mutation.

paragraphs.text: Retinitis pigmentosa-7 is a form of retinitis pigmentosa caused by mutation in the gene encoding peripherin/RDS, a photoreceptor cell-specific glycoprotein and the human homolog of the murine retinal degeneration slow (rds) gene (Kajiwara et al., 1991; Farrar et al., 1991). The disorder is usually transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait, but a digenic form occurs in individuals who are double heterozygotes for mutations in PRPH2 and ROM1 (Kajiwara et al., 1994). Manes et al. (2015) found that PRPH2 mutations cause highly variable phenotypes and moderate forms of autosomal dominant RP, with some affected members of a family having pericentral RP or macular dystrophy and others having widespread RP.

paragraphs.text: Weleber et al. (1993) described a family in which a 75-year-old woman, her 2 daughters (aged 44 and 50 years), and her 49-year-old son showed 3 different phenotypes. The mother presented at age 63 years with adult-onset retinitis pigmentosa and a profoundly abnormal ERG; over 12 years her disease progressed dramatically, with marked loss of peripheral visual field. One daughter developed pattern macular dystrophy at age 31 years; at age 44 her ERG was moderately abnormal, but her disease was limited to the macula. The other daughter presented with macular degeneration at age 42 years and over 10 years developed the picture of fundus flavimaculatus, with preserved peripheral field and a moderately abnormal ERG. The son had onset of macular degeneration at age 44 years, with pericentral scotomas, a markedly abnormal ERG, and punctate pigment epithelial transmission defects on fluorescein angiography.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2013) described 3 unrelated patients (1318, 3256, and 741) who were homozygous for PRPH2 missense mutations; 2 had Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) and 1 had juvenile RP. All had visual impairment within the first year of life, nondetectable or reduced ERGs, and a very similar maculopathy in the fundus. The 2 LCA patients also had nystagmus. Fundus findings included a multilobulated central atrophic maculopathy, vessel narrowing, peripheral pigment deposits or diffuse retinal dystrophy, and optic disc pallor in 1 patient.

paragraphs.text: Manes et al. (2015) found that disease severity was moderate in French patients with autosomal dominant RP and PRPH2 mutations: visual acuity was 1 to 0.5 in 78% of eyes, and 52% of eyes retained more than 50% of the visual field. Some patients characteristically had vitelliform deposits or macular involvement. Within some families, certain members had pericentral RP or macular dystrophy, whereas others had widespread RP. The authors concluded that PRPH2 mutations cause highly variable phenotypes and moderate forms of adRP, including mild cases that could be underdiagnosed.

paragraphs.text: Farrar et al. (1991) performed linkage analysis with chromosome 6p markers in an Irish pedigree with late-onset autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa. paragraphs.text: Using targeted next-generation sequencing of 163 retinal disease genes in patients with LCA or juvenile RP, Wang et al. (2013) found a homozygous c.554T-C transition in the PRPH2 gene, resulting in a leu185-to-pro (L185P) substitution, in LCA patient 3256; they noted that this mutation had previously been reported to cause digenic RP together with a ROM1 null mutation. Sequencing of PRPH2 in 135 additional unsolved patients identified the same homozygous L185P mutation in juvenile RP patient 741, whose parents were both heterozygous. Wang et al. (2013) also found a homozygous c.637T-C transition, resulting in a cys213-to-arg (C213R) substitution, in LCA patient 1318; this mutation had previously been associated with autosomal dominant pattern dystrophy. The patient's mother and son were heterozygous carriers, and an unaffected brother was homozygous wildtype. The mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
